# Betelgeuse Code

Short lessons on what really happens when code runs: the objects, the memory and the data structures inside
everyday Python and databases, and the ideas behind new results in computer science and maths, drawn step by step.
Each folder has the handout (PDF), a notebook you can run in seconds to look inside on your own machine, and the
code behind every picture.

| Lesson | What you'll see inside | Files |
|---|---|---|
| [How a Python dictionary finds a key: inside CPython’s hash table](hash-lookup/) | What `ages["leo"]` does inside CPython 3.12.7, read out of a real dictionary's memory: `hash()` turns the key into one big number, its last bits pick one of 8 slots, the slot points to one entry, and one key is compared; then the collision, the resize to 16 slots, and why a list can't be a key | [notes.pdf](hash-lookup/notes.pdf) · [notebook](hash-lookup/notebook.ipynb) · [code](hash-lookup/code/) |
| [How a database index finds a row: inside SQLite’s B-tree pages](db-index/) | What SQLite reads for one `WHERE email = ?`: the real pages, decoded from the database file, down the index's B-tree and the table's (1,000,000 rows, SQLite 3.45.3) | [notes.pdf](db-index/notes.pdf) · [notebook](db-index/notebook.ipynb) · [code](db-index/code/) |
| [What a Python list really holds: inside CPython’s list object](list-append/) | What `nums.append(7)` does inside a list: the slots read from memory and matched to `id()`, the spare room `sys.getsizeof` shows, a full block swapped for a bigger one, and the growth rule checked on 1,000 real appends (CPython 3.12.7) | [notes.pdf](list-append/notes.pdf) · [notebook](list-append/notebook.ipynb) · [code](list-append/code/) |
| [Inside the Riemann hypothesis: primes, zeros, and a proof only computers have read](riemann-hypothesis/) | The Riemann hypothesis in pictures and plain words, with the maths in boxes for the curious: the staircase of primes against Gauss's curve up to a trillion, Euler's sum built from the primes, zeta's zeros on the halfway line (the first at 14.13 up), the waves that rebuild the primes, a check you can run yourself to height 1,000 (649 zeros counted two ways), and what the computer check of November 20, 2026 did and did not establish | [notes.pdf](riemann-hypothesis/notes.pdf) · [notebook](riemann-hypothesis/notebook.ipynb) · [code](riemann-hypothesis/code/) |
| [Multiplying tables of numbers: Strassen, ω and OpenAI’s nine-fourths claim](matmul-exponent/) | Multiply two small tables by hand and count: 8 multiplications for 2 × 2, n³ for n × n. Strassen's 7 products and why one saved multiplication compounds on blocks (exponent log₂ 7 ≈ 2.807), what ω means and why it can't go below 2, the polynomial trick behind the 9/4 upper bound, the claimed floor ⌈n^(9/4)/2⌉, and exactly what was and wasn't checked as of 2026-11-25. Every count is made by numbers that tally their own multiplications | [notes.pdf](matmul-exponent/notes.pdf) · [notebook](matmul-exponent/notebook.ipynb) · [code](matmul-exponent/code/) |
